title: Eid al-Fitr: the day
hook: ghusl, perfume, best clothes, eating before prayer, a different road back (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last ten nights of Ramadan: the Prophet tightened his belt, brought the nights to life and woke his family. Now the month is over.

A small detail, tucked into Sahih al-Bukhari, in a report from Jabir. On the day of Eid, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, went out to the prayer by one road and came home by another. That's the whole report. No reason given. Just two roads. Before that walk, there's a morning to get through: water, clothes, something sweet to eat. Today, the morning of Eid al-Fitr, the feast that breaks the fast, one small act at a time.
screen: `ONE ROAD OUT.` → `ANOTHER ROAD BACK.` → `NO REASON GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Start with water. In the Muwatta of Imam Malik, Ibn 'Umar, a companion of the Prophet, would take a full bath, a ghusl, on the morning of the Fitr before going out to the prayer. The day begins clean. Then clothes. In al-Bukhari, 'Umar finds a fine cloak in the market and brings it to the Prophet, saying, in paraphrase: buy this, and dress up in it for Eid and for receiving visitors. The Prophet turned that one down, because it was silk. But notice what 'Umar took for granted: Eid is a day you dress for. For some, a little perfume too. Then food, and here's the surprise. Anas reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet would not go out on the day of the Fitr until he had eaten some dates, in an odd number. For a month, every fast broke at sunset. This one breaks in daylight, on purpose, before the prayer. Then the prayer itself, together with everyone. And then the road home, the different one. Why? Scholars have offered reasons: so both roads see the people of the day, so more neighbors get greeted, so more ground bears witness to the prayer. But Jabir only tells us what he did. The meaning is left open.
screen: `WATER: A GHUSL BEFORE GOING OUT.` · `CLOTHES: A DAY YOU DRESS FOR.` · `DATES BEFORE THE PRAYER.` · `A DIFFERENT ROAD HOME.`

segments.voice: In your mind, trace the way you usually come home: the turns, the corners, the same doors you've stopped noticing. Now find one other way, one street over or the long way round the park, and picture who might be on that road whom you never pass. If you pray, keep the Eid morning walk in mind; if you don't, simply keep the new road ready.
Eid al-Fitr. The feast that breaks the fast of Ramadan: a bath, good clothes, dates before the prayer, and a different road back. Today's word.
Your line: a new road home. The second road is still there to walk. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On the morning of Eid al-Fitr, Muslims often bathe, put on their best clothes, eat a few dates, and go to the Eid prayer together, and some take a different road home afterward, following a report in Sahih al-Bukhari.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the feast at the end of Ramadan.

trapdoor: what you thought: Eid is the party after Ramadan.
what it means: a morning with a shape: a bath, good clothes, dates before the prayer, the prayer together, and a different road home.
what a scholar hears: Ibn 'Umar's ghusl in the Muwatta, Anas on the dates and Jabir on the two roads in al-Bukhari, with the reason for the roads left unstated.

chat.says: Why do Muslims eat before the Eid prayer, right after a month of fasting?
options: The Prophet ate a few dates before going out; this fast breaks in daylight, on purpose.
They don't; the fast lasts until the Eid prayer is done, and then the meal starts.
Only the sick and travelers eat; everyone else keeps fasting through Eid day.
chat.meaning: Anas reports the Prophet wouldn't go out on the Fitr until he'd eaten some dates. Every fast broke at sunset; this one breaks in daylight.

Eid al-Fitr.meaning: the feast that breaks the fast of Ramadan

ghusl.meaning: a full ritual bath, as before the Eid prayer

Muwatta.meaning: Imam Malik's early collection of hadith and law

Jabir.meaning: the companion who reported the two roads

Anas.meaning: the companion who reported the dates before the prayer

notes: Confirm hadith numbers: Bukhari 986, 953, 948; and the Muwatta reference for Ibn 'Umar's ghusl.
Perfume is in the outline hook but no report is cited for it; the script says only 'for some, a little perfume too'. A Keeper may add a source or cut it.
The reasons offered for the different road are given as 'scholars have offered reasons'; confirm these are fairly represented (e.g., from Ibn Hajar's commentary in Fath al-Bari).
'Out in the open' for the Eid prayer: the Prophet's practice was at the musalla; many communities today pray in mosques or halls. Confirm the phrasing.
